questions.stem: In a GP clinic, you have told Minh Nguyen, 29, who has Crohn's disease, in plain words that his blood test shows long-term hepatitis B. He is anxious and asks: "Does this mean I can't have the new injection?" He wants treatment for his flare soon. Which response is best?
options: No; biologics aren't safe with hepatitis B, so we'll keep you on azathioprine alone.
Yes, after a short delay: an antiviral tablet starts first to keep the virus quiet.
Yes, straight away; your virus level is low, so it can't flare on the injection.
Not until the virus has fully cleared, which we'll recheck in about six months.
questions.why: Chronic hepatitis B is not a reason to refuse a biologic. Antiviral prophylaxis is started first, so the biologic comes after a short delay. Saying this answers his real worry honestly and without jargon.
notes: Hepatitis B does not rule out biologics once he has antiviral cover, and azathioprine can reactivate the virus too, so staying on it alone gives no protection.
A low HBV DNA does not protect him: anyone who is HBsAg positive can reactivate on immunosuppression, so the biologic must wait for antiviral cover.
Chronic hepatitis B rarely clears, so waiting for clearance would mean leaving his flare untreated with no end date. Antiviral cover is what lets treatment go ahead.

questions.stem: Minh Nguyen, 29, has Crohn's disease, takes azathioprine and is tapering prednisolone. He is about to start an anti-TNF agent. Results: HBsAg positive, total anti-HBc positive, IgM anti-HBc negative, HBeAg negative, HBV DNA 850 IU/mL, ALT 52 U/L, INR normal. Which hepatitis B plan is most appropriate?
options: Monitor HBV DNA and ALT 3-monthly; start an antiviral only if the DNA rises
Give a hepatitis B vaccine course and recheck anti-HBs before the biologic
Start lamivudine with the biologic and stop it once Crohn's is in remission
Start entecavir or tenofovir now; continue during and for 12+ months after
questions.why: Anyone who is HBsAg positive needs antiviral prophylaxis before immunosuppression, whatever the viral load. The choice is entecavir 0.5 mg or tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg daily, given throughout immunosuppression and for at least 12 months after it stops, as the specialist advises.
notes: Monitoring and acting only if the DNA rises is a plan for HBsAg-negative, anti-HBc-positive patients. In HBsAg-positive patients reactivation risk is high, so prophylaxis is needed.
He already has the infection (HBsAg positive), so vaccination cannot protect him. It is for his partner and household contacts if they are not immune.
Lamivudine quickly breeds resistance during long courses, and stopping it at remission is too early: reactivation can happen during and after immunosuppression.

questions.stem: Minh Nguyen, 29, has chronic hepatitis B, probably acquired from his mother at birth, with an HBV DNA of only 850 IU/mL. He asks why a virus at such a low level could cause a severe hepatitis once he starts biologic therapy. Which feature of hepatitis B biology best explains why it persists and can reactivate?
options: Covalently closed circular DNA stays in hepatocyte nuclei as a template for replication
Latent viral genomes persist in sensory ganglia and travel back along the axons
The virus persists mainly in B lymphocytes, which then expand once T-cell control is lost
Replication requires integration into host DNA, which steroids switch on directly
questions.why: HBV cccDNA sits as a stable minichromosome in the nuclei of infected hepatocytes, and antivirals do not remove it. When immunosuppression removes immune control, replication rises. The hepatitis that follows is caused by T cells destroying infected hepatocytes, often as immune function recovers.
notes: Latency in sensory ganglia is how herpesviruses such as varicella-zoster behave. HBV is hepatotropic and persists in hepatocytes.
Persistence in B cells describes Epstein-Barr virus. The HBV reservoir is the hepatocyte nucleus.
Integration of HBV DNA happens and contributes to HCC, but it is not needed for replication. The template for replication is cccDNA.

questions.stem: Minh Nguyen, 29, has ileocolonic Crohn's disease with cramping right-sided abdominal pain. On examination he has tenderness and fullness in the right iliac fossa, which fits terminal ileal disease. If he later needs an ileocaecal resection, which artery supplies the terminal ileum, caecum and appendix?
options: Right colic artery, arising directly from the superior mesenteric artery trunk
Middle colic artery, a branch of the superior mesenteric artery
Ileocolic artery, the terminal branch of the superior mesenteric artery
Left colic artery, a branch of the inferior mesenteric artery
questions.why: The ileocolic artery, the final branch of the SMA, supplies the terminal ileum, caecum and appendix (via the appendicular artery). It is the vessel divided in an ileocaecal resection for Crohn's disease.
notes: The right colic artery supplies the ascending colon, not the terminal ileum or caecum.
The middle colic artery supplies the transverse colon.
The IMA and its left colic branch supply the distal transverse colon and the descending colon, not the right iliac fossa bowel.
